extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency lawyers, and policy-makers interested in when agencies should use adjudication versus rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate when an agency should adopt policy through adjudication (orders) versus rulemaking, using legal standards, judicial doctrines, procedural considerations, and policy tradeoffs described in administrative-law scholarship and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using adjudication to make general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'choice to use adjudication to construct rules of general applicability can amount to an abuse of discretion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have overturned agency orders that effectively promulgated a general rule without examining specific facts or demonstrating particularized relevance to the adjudicated party. Example: First Bancorporation v. Board of Governors (10th Cir.)—agency 'examined no specific facts,' 'did not demonstrate' particularized relevance, and 'made no conclusions at all with respect to' underlying facts; result reversed as an abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness safeguards for adjudicatory policymaking
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies use adjudication to develop policy, courts require safeguards so litigants' cases are treated fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have instituted protections (due process review, examination of hearing sufficiency, and arbitrariness review) to ensure parties subject to adjudications receive fair treatment when orders have policymaking effect. Courts will assess whether there was 'such a want of hearing or such arbitrary or capricious action ... as to violate the due process clause.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish adjudicative facts from legislative facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudicative facts are facts concerning immediate parties; legislative facts inform a policy or legal judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Kenneth Culp Davis: when an agency finds facts concerning immediate parties it's performing an adjudicative function; when it wrestles with law or policy it's acting legislatively. This distinction matters for whether an agency may properly develop policy in an adjudication (adjudicative facts ground case-specific decisions; legislative facts are the proper basis for general rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking advances rule of law and democratic accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking is better for rule-of-law purposes and democratic accountability because it creates definite, publicly knowable standards and promotes like treatment under like circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and judges (e.g., Henry Friendly, David Shapiro) argue that rules make for even-handedness, reduce the chance agencies will depart from prior policy without explanation, and enable public understanding and accountability. The APA notice-and-comment process allows the public to participate and understand agency actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective notice and avoidance of retroactivity favor rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulated parties benefit from rulemaking because rules are prospective and reduce retroactive application of agency policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictability and stability ('definiteness' and 'degree of stability') let private actors plan economic decisions. Adjudication's case-by-case, retroactive nature can impose harsh effects on regulated parties; commentators urged agencies to inform those regulated of policy in advance (Warren Baker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking helps agencies frame policy and avoid capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking aids agency decisionmaking by allowing agencies to 'frame' policies, consider consequences, and maintain institutional independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Friendly and other scholars argued that rulemaking fosters deliberation, reduces policymaking by emotional or captured decisionmakers, and can 'supplant[] the original discretionary chaos ... with some degree of order' (Kenneth Culp Davis / American Hospital Ass'n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory language controls whether formal (on-the-record) procedures are required
rubrics_metrics.description: A statute that merely permits action 'after hearing' does not necessarily require APA formal (sections 556–557) on-the-record procedures; the statute must explicitly require 'on the record' to mandate formal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court decisions (United States v. Allegheny-Ludlum Steel Corp., United States v. Florida East Coast Ry. Co.) established a presumption favoring informal rulemaking: courts will not infer formal on-the-record procedures unless Congress's text clearly demands them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts police adjudicatory policymaking using due process and expansive jurisdictional facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have used constitutional due-process principles and a broad conception of 'jurisdictional facts' to curb overly aggressive adjudicatory policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges asked whether agencies provided hearings or acted arbitrarily/capriciously, and increasingly treated the line between law and fact as malleable so courts could overturn agency actions viewed as inappropriate; this judicial policing can limit agencies' use of adjudication to make policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication grounds policymaking in empirical, case-specific reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication 'grounds the agency’s decision-making in empirical reality' by requiring agencies to confront adjudicative facts rather than hypothetical or cherry-picked examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (Kenneth C. Davis) and the Supreme Court (Chenery II) observed that agencies may lack experience to convert tentative judgments into rigid rules; addressing issues through adjudication can provide the real-world experience needed before hardening policy into rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication can deliver speed and ex post clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudicatory policymaking can be faster than formal rulemaking and allows ex post case-by-case clarification of policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts have imposed protections that limit adjudication's sweep, adjudication still offers benefits like addressing actual facts, ex post clarification, additional (sometimes different) opportunities for public participation, and, importantly, speed compared to time-consuming formal adjudicatory procedures or lengthy rulemaking records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some regulatory schemes are better or legally required to be codified via rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex regulatory schemes are often better expressed in the Code of Federal Regulations; some policies are unwise or may be illegal to effectuate solely through adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cautions against trying to put all policy into adjudications—for example, developing a government reimbursement system via orders could be unwise and risk litigation over discriminatory payments. Certain statutes or policy types practically require promulgation in regulations rather than order-by-order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional statutes and agency mandates affect the choice of policymaking form
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress's creation of agencies and statutory rulemaking mandates (or lack thereof) influence whether agencies use adjudication or rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Congress created agencies (NHTSA, EPA, CPSC) with rulemaking responsibilities; changes in statutory mandates (e.g., FDA's expanded responsibilities 1962–1976) prompted agencies to issue regulations rather than rely on adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication risks indefinite, conflicting, or unstable standards if used for general policymaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Using adjudication to develop broad policy can produce indefinite or conflicting standards because decisions are made case-by-case rather than through a settled rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics observed that adjudication can allow agencies to deviate from prior policies without explanation, 'slip' policy changes into opinions without articulation, and maintain indefinite or conflicting standards so long as situations are handled separately; this undermines predictability and even-handedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural burden and practical speed tradeoffs shape method selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparative procedural burdens (e.g., formal adjudication's evidentiary hearings and cross-examination versus informal rulemaking's notice-and-comment) affect whether agencies choose adjudication or rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, informal rulemaking was comparatively fast and procedurally lax (short notices/final rules), while formal adjudication required evidence-gathering, trials, and full merits rulings that could take years; these practical differences influence agency choices.
